q: In a landmark move the supreme Court of India has issued a set of directives related to the application of section 498A of the Indian penal Code. Which of the following is not one of the directives?
options: In every district one or more family welfare committees be constituted
Every complaint under section 498A received by the police or the magistrate be referred to the family welfare committee
Till the report of the family welfare committee is received, no arrest should normally be effected
Supreme Court guidelines are not applicable in respect of persons ordinarily residing out of India.
key_text: Supreme Court guidelines are not applicable in respect of persons ordinarily residing out of India.
explanation:
the Family Welfare Committee directions were withdrawn in Social Action Forum v. Union of India (14 Sep 2018), and IPC 498A is now BNS s.85-86 (from 1 July 2024) — now no FWC filter before arrest (sci.gov.in)
In Rajesh Sharma v. State of UP (July 2017) the SC directed Family Welfare Committees in every district, referral of 498A complaints to them and no routine arrest before their report; it also covered NRIs (no routine impounding of passports/Red Corner Notices). So 'not applicable to persons residing out of India' was not a directive.

notes.text: - **Rajesh Sharma v. State of UP (2017):** Family Welfare Committees in every district; 498A complaints referred to them; no routine arrest before their report; NRIs also covered (no routine passport impounding).

explanation: Under s.5 of the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987 glorification of sati is punishable with 1 to 7 years and fine of ₹5,000-30,000; abetting sati carries death or life (s.3-4).
